title: Switching to trombone, a gig without a trumpet, credit to Paul Barbarin
summary: He switched to trombone at 15-16, recalls a trumpetless gig with a tuba, stresses always playing the melody, and credits Paul Barbarin for bringing him into New Orleans jazz.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: And how old were you when you switched over to trombone?
Well I was, I'd say 16 years old, between 15 and 16.
Did you ever play that in the school of Arkansas or were you about three of the school and you were?
But always wanted to play a funeral or parade like that but would never ever.
Yeah. And you remember your first job about on trombone? Well yeah I could.
Whose band it was? I don't remember the first job but I can tell you a funny job.

Well Mike Neal, Beau and I, and I forgot who the drummer was, trombone, bass, two and drum. We played a gig. Without a trumpet. Oh yeah, without a trumpet. Yeah, without a trumpet. See, I tell you, now that's one thing I remember what my dad always said, you know, is learn the melody to a tune, see. Then the amplifiers after. Yeah. Well I like, I had a lot of advantage because I mean, I did learn a little bit about the piano, you know. I learned the changes. But I always tried to play a melody to a tune. Always did.
Yeah that's one of the things most of the fellas in New Orleans tell us, that they try to always have that melody heard sometimes.

Yeah, but now Bill, this is the man's thing about this. Now, since this music got back, this New Orleans music got back, well I got to give credit to Paul Bobberman. That's the man that brought me in here. I didn't have much idea about it but I always liked it but I didn't have a chance to exercise it, you know. But Paul is the man. He's the man who really put me in this New Orleans jazz.
After that first, after you said it wasn't necessarily your first job with that one without a trumpet player, it wasn't a clarinet on the.
No, no, no, just a three piece of drum, bass, and who was the drum, I don't know, maybe Mac Neill probably, you know. But it was good, we was talking about that there the other night.
Did you stick to the melody most of the time or did you do variations too?
Well yeah, I amplified around the melody, you know, yeah.
Let the people know what's happening. What was the girl playing, string bass or?
Bass, bass tuba, one little small bass tuba.

Yeah, a little small one, you know. Uh huh. Because at that particular time they had a little band that called a question, say the high hatter. And uh, he was playing bass too. They had a pretty nice band then. School boy. And uh, they had another little band I was playing with. But we wasn't great as them though. But Paul is the man. He is.
